Hey guys. I've been around guns all my life, but they've been your standard handguns and hunting rifles/shotguns. .22, 30/30, 12 gauge, that sort of stuff. Remington, Marlin, Winchester. Manufactured by those well-known companies.

Now, I'm considering purchasing an assault rifle (apparently called "tactical rifle" these days) and getting more involved with shooting. In the 5.56 NATO versus the 7.62x39 war, I've decided on the 7.62. But in the non-hunting arena, there are so many different manufacturers that I know little/nothing about. Century Arms, Sig Sauer, Arsenal, H&K (I'm a little familiar with them), Norinco, etc.

And there are AK-47 clones everywhere when looking at firearms for this cartridge. I don't see many non-AK rifles in 7.62x39. I'd rather not get an AK, but I'm not totally opposed to it. In my totally uneducated opinion, I tend to prefer the G3-type rifles that PTR makes.

My question to you gentlemen is this: If you had approx. $1,000 to spend on a new/used 7.62x39 rifle, and weren't particularly fond of AKs, what rifles would you consider? What rifles would you stay the hell away from?
I'm looking to buy a 7.62x39 rifle, but I could use some direction

First off, an assault rifle is full auto. Does the gun you're trying to buy come with massive governmental restrictions to the point that it's not really worth the hassle, an artificially inflated $15,000+ price tag, and the ability to fire more than one bullet per trigger pull? If not, then it's just an AR or AK or SIG or whatever pattern rifle. "Tactical rifle" doesn't really mean much.

Second, G3 rifles are 7.62x51 NATO (also known as .308) and not 7.62x39, and these are two very different cartridges. The difference is that 7.62x51 is a full-sized rifle cartridge while 7.62x39 is an intermediate cartridge. You're looking at close to double the power out of 7.62x51 and it comes with everything associated with that power increase such as higher weight and lower magazine capacity. A military pattern, semi-automatic rifle that fires a full-sized rifle cartridge is properly termed a battle rifle; others include the FN FAL, the M14/Springfield M1A, and even things like the older M1 Garand. I'm assuming you actually want the 7.62x39 and just confused the two, but if you decide that you want a 7.62x51 battle rifle instead, any of the rifles I listed are good ones, despite the constant bitching about the M14 platform on the internet. I'd personally look at the FN FAL first, then the G3 pattern rifles like the PTR, then the M1A/M14.

Now, getting down to the core of your question. 7.62x39 rifles are plentiful but the vast, vast majority of them are AKs. Most of the remainder are SKS rifles of various descriptions. Arsenal are the best AK money can buy, but they're way on the expensive side. Century Arms are importers, most of their rifles are imported as parts kits and finished in the US so their quality varies wildly. Norinco can be OK, but they are Chinese rifles and they have been banned from import to the US for about 25 years now so any you find will have been in circulation for a while. Personally, my favorite AK pattern rifle is the Yugoslavian M70AB2 underfolder, they're easily the highest quality imported AKs and you can't go wrong with one of those. I just changed out the cheap, flimsy plastic handguards for wood ones on mine.

If you absolutely don't want an AK but are absolutely sold on 7.62x39, your only real choice is going to be the SKS. Look for a Russian SKS if you go that route, they're the best ones.

You can find AR15-style rifles in 7.62x39. If you want a serious, tactical-style rifle, I don't think you could beat that. There are some superb CZ bolt actions available in that caliber, too.

You can get some nice AK-style rifles if you want to spend the money, but if you really don't want an AK, then why bother? SKSs are historically interesting and they can be really good of what they are, as old-school, inexpensive, reliable carbines (the Russian Winchester 94), but they can't really be made into a high-end gun. The only sensible way to get $1000 worth of value out of an SKS is to buy the best one you can find, along with $700 worth of ammunition.

If your heart wants a G3 or some other modern tactical-style rifle, then you don't want a 7.62x39.

Personally, I'd get a Mutant or other such AR-inspired gun. The way to attach optics to them is simply superior to alternatives. Other than theese, you can look at Ruger Mini-30 or an SKS. If you like Czech exotics, look at Vz.52/57 in 7.62x39 or the Vz.58. Stay away from Rasheed, it was poorly designed in many small ways. I don't know of a roller-delayed gun in 7.62x39.

Remember that every time you choose to stick with traditional AK magazines, you lose the bolt hold-open function. But every time you choose a proprietary magazine, you screw yourself in the long run. So it's a balance.

On almost all the gun sites that I have visited I have noticed that how people view guns and all shooting activity represents where they live or where they grew up. Lets face it most of the population of the United States live east of the Mississippi river, or in California. The area east of the Mississippi river is for most part forest land with stands of deciduous or conifer trees and brush. It is quite natural that people coming or living there very rarely get to shoot over a couple of hundred yards. Also with the population density it is very dangerous to have rifles that have extremely long ranges. There fore (I think and I may be wrong) that people east of the Mississippi river tend to favor heavy slow moving projectiles that will buck brush over very high velocity smaller projectiles that will deflect on a blade of grass.

People like my self who grew up in Southern Idaho in the high desert where you can see water sprinklers in the early morning dawn 20 miles away, tend to pick rifles that extreme long range accuracy and killing power at those ranges. That may explain why the .30-06 is still the most popular hunting rifle for the high desert. When I was a kid, (Hell back then we would load our rigs on Friday morning and after school head out to the desert and be gone until Sunday afternoon. Hell it was common to see the pickups in the high school parking lots with all kinds of rifles and shotguns in the back window gun racks. I might add that I went to high school for four years where every body and their uncle was armed with all kinds of artillery and we never had a school shooting. Go Figure!!!

Any way, in the high desert no one thought it strange not to take a shot at a jack rabbit, rock chuck, Coyote at 400 yards. Even during deer season you rarely got a shot at a buck under 200 yards, Most deer were take between 200 and 400 yards with some (my step father one of them) taking a buck at 700 yards with a custom 06. So when some one talks about long range shooting I automatically assume that they grew up or live in the mountain west were long shots are the norm and not the exception.
